title: Cops Discover Dead Body in Man's Semi-Truck
description:

CONTACT US:
Complaints? Video submissions? Sponsorships? Collabs? Business inquires? 
Email our board at mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com. 

BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect. 

RIGHT TO BE FORGOTTEN:
Midwest Safety practices the "Right to be Forgotten." If you were the suspect in a lower-level offense, you may email our board to request removal. 
Email: mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com

The victim found dead inside the cab was 46-year-old Candace Thompson. Although the incident unfolded, in Maryland. Both were from Sickerville, New Jersey, and known to be domestic partners. According to investigators, their relationship had a documented history of domestic violence in Winslow Township. Thompson had suffered two large gashes to her back, and officers recovered a claw hammer and two folding knives from the driver's side door. Wattley was indicted on one count of first-degree murder and one count of second-degree murder. This is a call when you walk up thinking and it's just a welfare check, and then reality grabs you by the collar and says, brace yourself because this call is about to get really dark. That's policing, the moment you realize the call you plan for is not the call you walked into. There's a certain coldness in the air during the midnight shift that I know far too well. It's that feeling when your instincts start whispering before anyone even opens their mouth. The deputy was calm and playing it cool, but if you were paying attention, you can tell something just wasn't right. When a man refuses the simple things like water, a conversation, or even stepping out of a truck, it's never about the moment, it's about what he's hiding. Every cop has seen that look before that the suspect had, that silent something's wrong tension, the kind that makes the hairs on your arm actually stand up, and it's not fear, it's recognition. Then comes the discovery, the kind of doesn't need words, because it changes everything in the moment. And that's the kind of moment in policing with the noise around you just stops, because your brain takes about half a second to catch up to what your eyes are seeing. Because it's one thing to expect a fight, a chase, or a drunk driver. It's another thing entirely to realize you've just walked into someone's final chapter, and these are the calls that change cops forever. You hold the scene and you write your reports, but that image states etched in your mind even after retirement. My heart broke for this woman because this was a tragic ending. However, what's haunting to me is how much gets missed out there is simply because people, People assume the first glance tells the whole story.
